title: Fiat–Shamir heuristic
text:
For the algorithm specified below, readers should be familiar with the multiplicative groups \Z^*_q , where q is a prime number, and Euler's totient theorem on the Euler's totient function φ.

Here is an interactive proof of knowledge of a discrete logarithm in \Z^*_q , based on Schnorr signature.[1] The public values are y \in \Z^*_q and a generator g of \Z^*_q , while the secret value is the discrete logarithm of y to the base g.

Peggy wants to prove to Victor, the verifier, that she knows x satisfying y \equiv g^x without revealing x .

Peggy picks a random v\in \Z^*_q , computes t = g^v and sends t to Victor.

Victor picks a random c\in \Z^*_q and sends it to Peggy.

Peggy computes r = v - cx \bmod \varphi(q) and returns r to Victor.

Victor checks whether t \equiv g^ry^c . This holds because g^ry^c \equiv g^{v - cx}g^{xc} \equiv g^v \equiv t and g^{\varphi(q)} \equiv 1 .

Fiat–Shamir heuristic allows to replace the interactive step 3 with a non-interactive random oracle access. In practice, we can use a cryptographic hash function instead.[2]

Peggy wants to prove that she knows x such that y \equiv g^x without revealing x .

Peggy picks a random v\in\Z^*_q and computes t = g^v .

Peggy computes c = H(g,y,t) , where H is a cryptographic hash function.

Peggy computes r = v - cx \bmod \varphi(q) . The resulting proof is the pair (t,r) .

Anyone can use this proof to calculate c and check whether t \equiv g^ry^c .

If the hash value used below does not depend on the (public) value of y, the security of the scheme is weakened, as a malicious prover can then select a certain value t so that the product cx is known.[3]

Bellare, Mihir. (1995). Random Oracles are Practical: A Paradigm for Designing Efficient Protocols. ACM Press.
Bernhard, David. Advances in Cryptology – ASIACRYPT 2012.
